report.summary: Multiple kill criteria lack operational definitions, allowing formal compliance while defeating intent; e.g., 'beats' is undefined, 'equivalent' is subjective, and leakage prevention has no audit mechanism.
risks: 13.1 | high | 'does not beat' is undefined; an agent could define 'beat' as a non-statistically-significant margin or use a cherry-picked metric to avoid triggering the kill. | Require a pre-registered effect size and significance threshold per experiment.

13.2 | high | 'perform equivalently' is subjective; an agent could set a wide equivalence margin or use a low-powered test to conclude equivalence even when real differences exist. | Pre-specify equivalence bounds and power analysis.
13.3 | high | 'perform equivalently' again subjective; same as above. | Same fix as 13.2.

13.4 | medium | 'no marginal contribution' is vague; an agent could define contribution as non-zero improvement on a noisy metric, or use an ablation that removes multiple components at once. | Require per-component ablation with statistical testing.

13.5 | high | 'does not predict or cause' conflates correlation with causation; an agent could claim no causal link by using a weak intervention or insufficient data. | Require a specific causal inference method (e.g., do-calculus, RCT).
13.6 | high | 'does not beat' again undefined; also 'random or evaluator-only choice' is ambiguous (e.g., random with what distribution?). | Pre-register baselines and comparison protocol.

13.7 | medium | 'scrubbing' method not specified; an agent could use a weak scrubbing procedure that leaves leakage intact, then claim gain persists. | Define scrubbing requirements (e.g., temporal holdout, time-series cross-validation).

13.8 | medium | 'explain the whole gain' is vague; an agent could attribute gain to context tokens via a simple correlation without controlling for other factors. | Require a controlled experiment adding extra tokens to baseline.

13.9 | high | 'worsens the quality/cost frontier' is undefined; an agent could define a frontier that always favors their method by choosing a specific cost metric or weighting. | Pre-register cost metric and frontier definition.
13.10 | medium | 'usable cost' is subjective; an agent could set an arbitrarily high cost threshold to avoid kill. | Define cost constraints in terms of user tolerance or budget.
13.11 | high | 'useful precision' is undefined; an agent could set precision threshold very low or use a biased evaluation set. | Pre-register precision target and evaluation dataset.
13.12 | medium | 'benefits disappear' is vague; an agent could require zero benefit or use a narrow set of repositories/tasks. | Pre-register a diverse set of held-out repositories and tasks.

13.13 | medium | 'seal the evaluator from the candidate' is not mechanically defined; an agent could leave side channels (e.g., shared logs, time correlation). | Require a specific blinding protocol (e.g., separate machines, no shared state).

13.14 | medium | 'identical problem definitions' is impossible to guarantee across task classes; an agent could vary problem formulation in subtle ways. | Require a formal problem specification language.
13.15 | medium | 'compute/token budgets' are not enforced; an agent could count tokens differently or use hidden compute. | Require logging and auditing of resource usage.
13.16 | low | 'multiple task classes' is vague; an agent could choose easy tasks within each class. | Require a pre-registered task suite with difficulty levels.
13.17 | medium | '5-10 seeds' is a guideline, not a rule; an agent could run 5 seeds and claim compliance even if variance is high. | Require power analysis to determine number of seeds.
13.18 | medium | 'Report ... separately' is not enforced; an agent could omit unfavorable metrics or combine them in a misleading way. | Require a standardized reporting template.

13.19 | medium | 'Reject results when ... changed together' is not operationalized; an agent could change multiple things and claim each was controlled. | Require a factorial experimental design or ablation.
13.20 | high | Leakage prevention list is exhaustive but no audit mechanism; an agent could inadvertently leak and not detect it. | Require automated leakage detection tools and logging.

13.21 | medium | 'model-generated hypotheses re-entering the Knowledge plane as facts' is a specific leakage but no control mechanism specified. | Require a separate fact-checking step or provenance tracking.
todos: Define 'beat' and 'perform equivalently' with pre-registered statistical thresholds and equivalence margins.
Specify concrete causal inference methods for 'predict or cause'.
Define scrubbing procedures and require automated leakage detection.
Pre-register cost metrics, frontier definitions, and precision targets.
Require a formal experimental design protocol (e.g., factorial designs, power analysis).
Add auditing and logging requirements for resource usage and blinding.

claims.claim: The full representation does not beat code-only or BM25 retrieval.
claims.why: The term 'beat' is not defined. An agent could claim that a non-significant improvement or a small margin on a cherry-picked metric counts as beating, thus avoiding the kill criterion. The rule cannot detect this because it does not specify what constitutes beating.

claims.claim: Degree-preserving randomized cross-plane edges perform equivalently.
claims.why: 'Perform equivalently' is subjective. An agent could set a wide equivalence margin or use a low-powered test to conclude equivalence even when real differences exist. The rule does not specify equivalence bounds or statistical tests.

claims.claim: Four independent indices perform equivalently to cross-plane fusion.
claims.why: Same issue as 13.2; 'perform equivalently' is subjective. No operational definition of equivalence.

claims.claim: A plane has no marginal contribution in ablation.
claims.why: 'No marginal contribution' is vague. An agent could define contribution as any non-zero improvement on a noisy metric, or perform ablation that removes multiple components at once, making it unclear which component contributed. The rule does not specify how to measure marginal contribution.

claims.claim: Graph movement does not predict or cause behavioral improvement.
claims.why: 'Does not predict or cause' conflates correlation and causation. An agent could claim no causal link by using a weak intervention (e.g., small perturbation) or insufficient data. The rule does not specify a causal inference method.

claims.claim: Graph-conditioned prioritization does not beat random or evaluator-only choice.
claims.why: 'Does not beat' is undefined, and 'random or evaluator-only choice' is ambiguous (e.g., random with what distribution? evaluator-only with what policy?). An agent could choose a weak baseline to avoid being beaten. The rule does not specify baselines or comparison protocol.

claims.claim: The gain disappears after temporal and knowledge-leakage scrubbing.
claims.why: 'Scrubbing' method is not specified. An agent could use a weak scrubbing procedure that leaves leakage intact, then claim the gain persists. The rule does not define what constitutes adequate scrubbing.

claims.claim: Extra context tokens explain the whole gain.
claims.why: 'Explain the whole gain' is vague. An agent could attribute gain to context tokens via a simple correlation without controlling for other factors. The rule does not require a controlled experiment where extra tokens are added to the baseline.

claims.claim: Graph construction/query cost worsens the quality/cost frontier.
claims.why: 'Worsens the quality/cost frontier' is undefined. An agent could define a frontier that always favors their method by choosing a specific cost metric (e.g., ignoring latency) or weighting. The rule does not specify how the frontier is defined or measured.

claims.claim: Revision-atomic snapshots cannot be maintained at usable cost.
claims.why: 'Usable cost' is subjective. An agent could set an arbitrarily high cost threshold to avoid the kill criterion. The rule does not define cost constraints.

claims.claim: Embedding proposals cannot achieve useful precision after verification cost.
claims.why: 'Useful precision' is undefined. An agent could set a very low precision threshold or use a biased evaluation set to claim the criterion is not met. The rule does not specify precision targets or evaluation protocol.

claims.claim: Benefits disappear on held-out repositories, under equal context budgets, or in cross-project transfer.
claims.why: 'Benefits disappear' is vague. An agent could require zero benefit or use a narrow set of repositories/tasks. The rule does not specify what constitutes 'disappear' (e.g., no statistically significant improvement) or the diversity of held-out data.

claims.claim: Seal the evaluator from the candidate.
claims.why: The instruction is not mechanically defined. An agent could leave side channels (e.g., shared logs, time correlation) and claim compliance because no explicit rule was violated. The rule does not specify a blinding protocol.

claims.claim: Use identical problem definitions and compute/token budgets.
claims.why: 'Identical problem definitions' is impossible to guarantee across different task classes; an agent could vary problem formulation in subtle ways (e.g., different prompt templates). The rule does not require a formal problem specification.

claims.claim: Use identical compute/token budgets.
claims.why: Budgets are not enforced; an agent could count tokens differently (e.g., exclude system prompts) or use hidden compute (e.g., precomputation). The rule does not require logging or auditing of resource usage.

claims.claim: Cover multiple task classes.
claims.why: 'Multiple task classes' is vague; an agent could choose easy tasks within each class and claim coverage. The rule does not specify the number or difficulty of tasks.

claims.claim: Run at least 5–10 seeds when stochastic variance matters.
claims.why: This is a guideline, not a rule; an agent could run 5 seeds and claim compliance even if variance is high and more seeds are needed. The rule does not require a power analysis to determine the appropriate number of seeds.

claims.claim: Report algorithm quality, sample efficiency, repository evolution, and product reliability separately.
claims.why: The instruction is not enforced; an agent could omit unfavorable metrics or combine them in a misleading way. The rule does not specify a standardized reporting template or require all metrics to be reported.

claims.claim: Reject results when code, prompts, memory, model, search policy, and evaluator changed together.
claims.why: This is not operationalized; an agent could change multiple things and claim each was controlled (e.g., by doing a series of pairwise comparisons). The rule does not require a factorial experimental design or ablation to isolate effects.

claims.claim: Prevent leakage from gold patches, private tests, post-cutoff issue/commit text, post-task graph edges, previous solutions in adaptive memory, base/candidate snapshot mixing, evaluator paths or outputs.
claims.why: The list is exhaustive but no audit mechanism is specified; an agent could inadvertently leak and not detect it. The rule does not require automated leakage detection tools or logging of data flows.

claims.claim: Prevent leakage from model-generated hypotheses re-entering the Knowledge plane as facts.
claims.why: This is a specific leakage type but no control mechanism is specified. An agent could allow such re-entry if not explicitly prevented. The rule does not require a separate fact-checking step or provenance tracking.
